findings.passage: and then explained the act as protection rather than as rage or proof of toughness.
findings.problem: This misstates his answer. In S1 (opened), Oprah asks whether his father's leaving turned him into 'the kind of angry kid who would end up shooting his brother'. He answers 'Yes—and my brother was dealing with a lot of demons', then gives Eric's age and says he 'needed to protect everybody.' He accepted anger and added protection as context. He did not offer protection instead of rage. The sentence presents his most violent self-reported act in the thesis's protective frame and erases an admission he actually made. The claim inventory gets this right (C28: 'He accepts anger as part of the act'), but the prose does not.
findings.acceptance_test: The passage reports that he answered 'Yes' to the anger question and added his brother's drug use and his wish to protect the family as context. No sentence says he framed the shooting as protection rather than rage. The wording matches C28's inference.

findings.passage: He let West talk about him "100 times," then went silent when West named his wife.
findings.problem: The sequence is unsupported, and it assigns him a motive he did not state. West's Sacramento speech (S14, opened) already says 'You still ain't calling me', so Jay-Z's silence was in place when West talked about Beyonce, not caused by it. On Rap Radar (S5, opened), Jay-Z says bringing in 'my kids and my wife' made it 'a real, real problem'. He does not date his silence to that moment. This sentence sits in the discriminator section, so the invented sequence becomes type evidence.
findings.acceptance_test: The discriminator attributes the line to Jay-Z: on Rap Radar in August 2017 he said that bringing in his family ('my kids and my wife') was what made it 'a real, real problem.' No sentence says his silence began when West named Beyonce. If the silence is mentioned, the article notes that West's own November 2016 speech shows it was already in place.

findings.passage: His account still matches Jay-Z's own word for his younger self, "cold," and it matches the pattern: when control of the work was at stake, the friendship did not decide the outcome.
findings.problem: The draft turns a hostile witness's insult into corroboration by matching one word. Jay-Z's 'really quiet and really cold' (S1) describes an 11-year-old's emotional withdrawal after his father left. Dash's 'He's cold' (S13, opened; verbatim, slur removed) charges an adult with business ruthlessness. These are different claims. The section also drops Dash's own structural explanation in the same interview: 'That's the algorithm... They make one sell out the other, their friend, divide and conquer'. It gives no response or position from Jay-Z on the betrayal charge, and it omits that the 2021 NFT suit ended in a June 2022 settlement (per S13). 'The friendship did not decide the outcome' is author inference, stated as fact.
findings.acceptance_test: The section no longer presents the shared word 'cold' as corroboration, or it explicitly notes that the two uses mean different things. Dash's industry-pressure framing appears in his words. The article either gives Jay-Z's sourced account of the 2004 split or states that the profile found no public response from him. The control-over-friendship conclusion is marked as interpretation. The NFT suit is described as settled. In 'What separates them', the masters condition is attributed ('he says he made...'), because it is his self-report and Dash disputes the episode.

findings.passage: Asked why Kaepernick was not part of it, Jay-Z said, "You'd have to ask him. I'm not his boss."
findings.problem: The truncation changes the tone of his answer. S7 (opened) continues: 'I can't just bring him into something. That's for him to say.' It also reports that he said he and Kaepernick had talked about the deal. Cut short, the answer reads as dismissive, when he was deferring to Kaepernick's choice. The Type 3 section also omits his stated reason for the partnership, which S7 reports at length: 'the kneeling was not about a job, it was about injustice', 'how do we address that injustice?', 'the NFL has a huge platform and we can use that huge platform', and the Inspire Change program. S7 also says he 'has been among the biggest supporters of Kaepernick.' Without that, the reader gets only the author's 'a Three choosing the bigger platform' reading and Reid's criticism, never his own explanation.
findings.acceptance_test: The Kaepernick answer is quoted in full or paraphrased faithfully, including that he said it was Kaepernick's call and that the two had spoken. At least one sentence gives his stated social-justice reason for the deal, in his own words from S7. The 'bigger platform' interpretation appears alongside that reason and is labeled as interpretation.

findings.passage: What he refused in 2019 was the audition: being one of four names waiting to be chosen.
findings.problem: The hook, persona title ('The Man Who Won't Audition'), meta description ('turned down the Super Bowl because it felt like an audition') and the discriminator ('he refused the halftime show because it meant waiting to be picked') all treat dislike of auditioning as the established reason for his refusals. That is his stated reason at the August 2019 press conference. But the same source (S7) frames his earlier refusals inside the Kaepernick context: he had 'turned down invitations to perform at the Super Bowl, even rapping about it in a song,' and was 'among the biggest supporters of Kaepernick.' The refusals were widely read as solidarity, which is exactly why the 2019 partnership drew hypocrisy charges. Dropping that context swaps in the author's motive for a publicly contested one and hides why critics saw the deal as a reversal.
findings.acceptance_test: The body labels 'didn't like the process' as his 2019 stated explanation. It notes, with a source, that his earlier refusals had been publicly tied to his support for Kaepernick, and that he rapped about refusing. Any added lyric must come from an opened source and be logged as a claim. The meta description, persona title, FAQ and discriminator do not present audition aversion as the sole established motive. For example, the description says he 'said' the process felt like an audition.

findings.passage: ## The record he does not narrate
findings.problem: The heading accuses him of evading or concealing these episodes, and the section's own evidence contradicts it. The draft quotes his Decoded account of the stabbing ('a mindless assault'). It also quotes his public statement on the lawsuit, and S15 reports that he 'strongly denied the claims in both public statements and in court filings.' Putting an 'unnarrated' frame on a voluntarily dismissed allegation of sexually assaulting a 13-year-old suggests he is hiding something. That is the most harmful overclaim in the draft, and it cuts against the section's careful statement that neither episode is used as type evidence.
findings.acceptance_test: The heading is neutral and implies no silence, avoidance or concealment (for example, 'Two disputed episodes'). No sentence in the section suggests he has declined to address either matter.

findings.passage: In a statement, Jay-Z called the claims "frivolous, fictitious and appalling" and said "the trauma that my wife, my children, loved ones and I have endured can never be dismissed."
findings.problem: His response is incomplete on the point readers most often get wrong. ABC (S15, opened) reports his attorney Alex Spiro saying he 'never settled, he never paid 1 red penny,' and that Carter accused Buzbee of an 'extortionate campaign' in court filings. Without the no-settlement point, 'voluntarily dismissed' can read as a quiet payout. If the edit adds the extortion and defamation fight, S16 shows it is still live and time-sensitive: a Texas judge dismissed Roc Nation's claims against former Buzbee clients in June 2026, Buzbee said he would appeal, and Jay-Z's defamation case was proceeding separately.
findings.acceptance_test: The section includes an attributed statement that the case ended without a settlement or payment, per his attorney in February 2025. Any mention of his countersuits is dated, gives their June 2026 status from S16, and is logged as a time_sensitive or unresolved claim with a review trigger.

findings.passage: He also warned Oprah about himself: "I'm not normally a talkative person. I don't have conversations like this for no reason."
findings.problem: 'Warned' gives the line a meaning it does not have in context. In S1 (opened) he is explaining that music is his outlet: 'When you make music, you're constantly on the psychiatrist's couch, so to speak. That's an outlet for me. Because I'm not normally a talkative person.' It is not a caution about how far to trust his self-reports. The lines just before it ('If I were to act as if what I did wasn't bad, that would be irresponsible. And I'd have to bear the weight of that.') are his moral accounting of his dealing years, and the profile leaves them out while quoting 'addicted to the lifestyle' in the Type 3 case.
findings.acceptance_test: The quote is framed as he meant it (music as his outlet, talking as unusual for him), or it is cut. 'Warned' is gone. Optionally, his acknowledgment that dealing was wrong appears where his dealing years are discussed.

protected_passages.passage: These accounts are his own, and a frightened child in a violent neighborhood is not a personality type.
protected_passages.reason: Exemplary fairness. It separates self-report from inference and refuses to turn childhood trauma into typing evidence.

protected_passages.passage: The limit is plain: the 2017 and 2018 versions came in the years after _Lemonade_, when repairing a public image was also in his interest. Both readings agree that he changed. They disagree about why.
protected_passages.reason: States the strongest self-interest reading of his therapy and infidelity accounts without accusing him of insincerity. Keep this honest limit next to the thesis.

protected_passages.passage: The court record and the victim's later account do not agree, and this profile does not choose between them.
protected_passages.reason: Handles the stabbing fairly: the guilty plea, Decoded and Rivera's 2023 denial are all present, and nothing is resolved by authorial fiat.

protected_passages.passage: An allegation and a denial tell us nothing about his personality, and they are noted here only for accuracy.
protected_passages.reason: The right firewall between a dismissed allegation and the type argument. Keep it as the heading changes.

protected_passages.passage: The answer fits, but it is also convenient, and a reader can reasonably weigh the quiet more heavily than this profile does.
protected_passages.reason: Admits that the reconciling interpretation is convenient and leaves the reader room to disagree. Rare and valuable.

assessment: Fairness proxy. I did not speak for Jay-Z. I opened S1 (via r.jina.ai; oprah.com returns 403 to curl), S5, S7, S11, S13, S14 and S15 to check the passages that bear on fairness. Overall the draft is careful. It separates self-report from inference in most places, flags its reliance on friendly or promotional interviews, presents both disputed episodes with responses, keeps them out of the type argument, and leaves out the Letterman material about his mother's sexuality, which belongs to her. The problems cluster where the prose bends the record toward the protective-Eight thesis or toward the Three case. It turns his 'Yes' to anger into 'protection rather than rage' (subject-1). It invents a sequence for his silence toward West (subject-2). It uses a one-word match to turn Dash's hostile insult into corroboration while omitting Dash's own structural explanation and any response from Jay-Z (subject-3). It truncates his Kaepernick answer and drops his stated reason for the NFL deal (subject-4). It treats audition aversion as the settled motive for the halftime refusals, though the same source puts them in a Kaepernick-solidarity context (subject-5). The worst single framing is the heading that calls a dismissed allegation of child sexual assault part of 'the record he does not narrate' (subject-6). He denied it publicly and in court, and the section quotes him doing so. None of these is a blocker, but subject-1 through subject-5 touch the hook, title or discriminator, so the type argument should be re-read once they are fixed. Risks: sensitive_allegations and contested_typing stay true. I add no historical-source risk. A thesis change is not required, though fixing subject-5 should soften the persona title and description. The similarity advisory tripped only on the shared phrase 'Eight read(ing)' with Nara-Smith. That is ordinary type vocabulary, and the arguments differ, so I record no reuse finding.
